finding.claim: deleteAccount computes the authorization decision with canDelete(u, a) but discards the result, so any caller can delete any account by id (broken object-level authorization / IDOR).
finding.source: Attacker-controlled path parameter `id` in DELETE /accounts/{id} (comment at line 19), combined with any authenticated user `u`.
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at line 23, a protected state-changing operation.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) entry point; u is the caller, id comes from the URL.
Account a = accounts.get(id) loads the target by attacker-chosen id with no owner/tenant scoping.
canDelete(u, a) is evaluated but its boolean result is ignored; no throw, no if, no assertion.
accounts.remove(id) executes unconditionally, deleting the account regardless of ownership.
The predicate itself (u.admin() || a.ownerId() == u.id()) is correct, so the defect is solely non-enforcement at line 22.

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (line 10) computes correct admin-or-owner logic but is not enforced at line 22. closeAccount (line 29, assertCanDelete throws) is the enforced pattern that deleteAccount should match. No HTTP-layer auth guard is present in this repo, so route-level authentication could not be verified; the finding assumes an authenticated non-admin caller can reach the route. If a framework enforces ownership before this call, impact is reduced, but no such check is visible here. Also, a missing account yields NPE at line 10 for non-admin callers, which is a 500 rather than a bypass.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete at src/AccountService.java:9-11 returns a bool, but its result is discarded as a bare statement at line 22, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs unconditionally. The enforced pattern, assertCanDelete (lines 13-17, throws), is used only by closeAccount (line 29), not deleteAccount. No HTTP-layer auth or ownership check exists in the repo (only the comment at line 19).
verdict.reason: At src/AccountService.java:22 the boolean from canDelete(u, a) is discarded, so the removal at line 23 runs for any caller `u` who supplies any id, while closeAccount at line 29 correctly uses assertCanDelete, which throws. Every trace line matches the code. The only residual uncertainty is whether a framework outside this repo enforces the route, which I cannot see; within the available code the attacker needs only a User value, which is a low-privilege authenticated role.
